Chapter 55: Redundancy, Repair, and Maintenance Debt

Substitution and intervention are different strategies—and postponed work does not vanish.

Here the focus is parallel redundancy under independence, steady availability as uptime fractions, and maintenance debt as an accumulating obligation.

Finite Envelopes

Constant-hazard survival forms were already used in Chapters 20 and 45; they describe continued existence under conditions, not permanence under all futures. Landauer’s bound for ideal erasure of one unbiased bit at temperature T is Q_min = k_B T ln 2 (about 2.871×10⁻²¹ J at 300 K)—already noted earlier in the book—and does not price ordinary retention or every operation.

Parallel Redundancy Versus Repair

For n identical independent units each with horizon reliability R, a parallel-OR architecture that needs any one up has

R_parallel = 1 − (1 − R)^n

only under that architecture and independence; switching and common-mode faults are separate caveats.

For a repairable alternating up/down process with finite positive mean up time t̄_up and mean down time t̄_down, the long-run availability

A = t̄_up / (t̄_up + t̄_down)

is the limiting fraction of time spent up—not a survival probability over a fixed window. Definitions of “MTBF” vary across industries; the up/down means above keep the accounting explicit.

Figure 55.1. Parallel-OR reliability 1−(1−R)^n for identical independent units, R=0.9, n=1…5. Architecture toy—not a measured plant.

Maintenance Debt

Treat debt D (toy backlog units) with D ≥ 0, constant accrual rate A, and maintenance rate M. While D > 0,

dD/dt = A − M;

at D = 0 the floor rule is dD/dt = max(A − M, 0), so debt cannot go negative. Figure 55.2 uses A = 1, initial D(0) = 2, and compares M = 0.6 (debt grows) with M = 1.2 (debt declines until the floor). Under these toy assumptions, D is a quantified backlog—not a universal engineering standard.

Figure 55.2. Debt D(t) with A=1, D(0)=2: M=0.6 (grows) vs M=1.2 (declines to floor 0). Toy ODE—not a backlog audit.

Maintenance versus replacement when defining invariants fail was already the identity theme of Chapters 26 and 43.

Thesis

Redundancy substitutes; repair intervenes; debt accumulates when intervention lags accrual. Availability numbers inherit the up/down definitions used to compute them.

Place to Explore

For R=0.9, compute R_parallel for n=2 and n=3 under independence. Separately, with t̄_up = 99 and t̄_down = 1, compute the long-run availability A and the down fraction 1 − A. Distinguish that 99% availability from the (unspecified here) probability of no break over 100 time units, which would need a failure-time model.

Connections

Chapter 20 treated maintenance budgets and Weibull populations; Chapter 20 treated repair trajectories; Chapter 39 treated common-mode cuts.

Chapter 56: Material Memory, Many Clocks, and the Choice Among Repairs

A system is as old as the part that fails first, and repairing it is a decision with a horizon.

Principles 1120–1124 deal with memory stored in materials, components that age on different clocks, the economics of repair, the survival of essential functions under scarcity, and the passage from survival to renewal. The source previewed them at the close of the previous thread and develops them in this one. This chapter adds what the Maxwell model predicts at fixed strain and at fixed stress, why a weighted condition score can look healthy while the whole system is likely to have failed, and how the horizon decides between repairing and replacing. Chapter 18 already audited the same Maxwell relation from an earlier principle (1083), and Chapter 20 and Chapter 55 hold the damage balance and maintenance debt that this chapter builds on.

What a Material Remembers

The source says that a material’s previous experiences can alter its present structure and its response to future conditions (1120). It lists four carriers of such memory: entangled dislocations that raise resistance to further deformation through work hardening, residual stresses that remain after the load that produced them is gone, magnetic domains that keep a configuration after the field is removed, and viscoelastic polymers whose response depends on how fast and how long they were loaded. These are correct, and its failure mode is the useful part: two pieces with identical shape and dimensions need not have identical internal states.

Its viscoelastic example is the Maxwell model, a spring of modulus E in series with a dashpot of viscosity η, dε/dt=(dσ/dt)/E+σ/η. The source says the model describes stress relaxation and creep “under appropriate conditions”. That needs a split. Hold the strain fixed and the stress relaxes exponentially, σ(t)=σ₀e^(−t/τ) with τ=η/E. With E=1 GPa and η=10^12 Pa s, τ=1000 s; after 1000 s the stress has fallen to e^(−1)≈0.368 of its initial value, and it reaches a tenth after τ ln 10≈2303 s. Hold the stress fixed instead and the model predicts strain that grows without limit, ε(t)=σ/E+σt/η: with σ=1 MPa the strain is 0.001 at once and 0.002 after 1000 s, and it keeps rising linearly. Many solid polymers show creep that slows and is partly recovered on unloading; the Maxwell element cannot describe that, and models such as the Kelvin–Voigt element or the standard linear solid are used instead.[93] The model is a good account of relaxation in a material that flows, and a poor account of creep in one that does not.

Figure 56.1. Left: Maxwell stress relaxation at fixed strain for τ=η/E=1000 s and 250 s; the grey line marks one tenth of the initial stress. Right: three components with exponential lifetimes of mean 10, 30 and 100 years and weights 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6. The weighted condition score stays near 0.66 at 20 years while the probability that all three still work is about 0.057. Idealized models.

One System, Several Clocks

The source says that different components age at different rates, so no single clock describes a system (1121): paint, roofing and foundations; molecular turnover, cellular repair and organism-level aging. Its table of characteristic times is labelled illustrative, and its warning is the right one: a structure can look healthy because its longest-lived parts are intact while a short-lived, critical part has failed.

It then proposes an overall condition Q(t)=Σw_i q_i(t) and notes that dependencies can make the relationship nonlinear. The weighted sum is not merely approximate when parts are critical; it answers a different question. Give three components exponential lifetimes with means 10, 30 and 100 years and weights 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6. At 20 years the survival probabilities are e^(−2)≈0.135, e^(−2/3)≈0.513 and e^(−0.2)≈0.819, and the weighted score is about 0.659. If all three are needed, the probability that the system still works is their product, about 0.057. The hazards add, 1/10+1/30+1/100≈0.143 per year, so the system’s mean life is about 6.98 years: shorter than that of its shortest-lived component.[94] A weighted average describes how much of the inventory remains. Only a structure function, series, parallel or something in between, describes whether the whole still works (Chapter 40).

Repair, Restoration, Replacement

The source distinguishes four strategies: maintenance, which slows deterioration; repair, which restores a damaged component or function; restoration, which returns a system to a specified earlier condition; and replacement (1122). It writes a lifecycle cost C_total=C_initial+C_maintenance+C_repair+C_failure+C_retirement and says the choice depends on expected costs over the relevant period, and on safety, historical significance, reliability and the preservation of original evidence. Its caution that a restored object is not the same physical object in every respect, so restoration claims must be precise, is Chapter 80’s evidenced lineage.

Two terms in that sum need care. The failure cost is an expectation, probability times consequence. Costs that arrive in different years are not added at face value but discounted (Chapter 82). Take a toy comparison. Repair costs 2 now and leaves a component with annual maintenance 1.5 and a yearly failure probability of 0.10 with consequence 20, an expected 3.5 per year. Replacement costs 15 and leaves maintenance 0.5 and failure probability 0.01, an expected 0.7 per year. At a 5% discount rate the ten-year present cost of repair is 2+3.5×7.722≈29.0 and of replacement 15+0.7×7.722≈20.4, so replacement is cheaper. Over three years the annuity factor is 2.723 and the order reverses: about 11.5 against 16.9. The two options cost the same when the annuity factor reaches 13/2.8≈4.64, a horizon of about 5.4 years. The source’s statement that the decision depends on the period is correct, and the arithmetic shows how strongly it can depend on it. A cost comparison is complete only when its horizon and discount rate are stated.

What Must Remain

The source says that under scarcity, survival may depend on separating essential functions from secondary capabilities, which is the logic of graceful degradation (1123). A spacecraft under a power shortfall protects navigation, communication, thermal control and power, and suspends optional experiments. Its allocation identity, R_available=ΣR_i, should be an inequality, ΣR_i≤R_available, with minimum requirements for the functions that cannot be suspended. The test that matters is whether the sum of those minimums fits inside the budget. If it does not, no allocation preserves the system, and the question becomes which function to lose. The source’s examples, a hospital optimizing throughput at the expense of care and an archive that keeps its interface but neglects file integrity, are the proxy failure of Chapter 29 and Chapter 90. Its reframed question, which functions must stay available for the system to keep serving its purpose, is the right one, and it puts the decision about purpose before the scarcity rather than during it.

From Survival to Renewal

The source says that renewal uses the consequences of a system’s history to build a new viable organization. A forest after disturbance recycles nutrients and opens space, and the new forest is not a copy of the old (1124). Its transition map S_(t+1)=F(S_t,E_t,R_t,N_t) is a statement of dependence, not a model to compute with. Its checklist—what remains useful, what must be repaired, replaced or retired, what evidence must be kept, and what possibilities must stay open—is sound. Its failure mode is the important correction to a common hope: collapse does not guarantee renewal, and breakdown can destroy the resources and relationships a successor would need. Chapter 61 showed that the successor of a tipped system is usually a different state rather than the original, and Chapter 77 gives renewal as a balance of rates. The source’s closing sequence, from formation through maintenance, degradation, repair or transformation, to renewal or retirement, is offered as non-linear, and it should be read that way.

Thesis

A material’s history lives in its internal state, a system is only as healthy as its critical parts allow, and the choice between repairing and replacing is decided by the horizon and discount rate, which therefore have to be stated before the costs are compared.

Place to Explore

A Maxwell material has E=1 GPa and η=10^12 Pa s. Find its relaxation time and the time for the stress at fixed strain to fall to one tenth. Three essential components have exponential lifetimes with means 10, 30 and 100 years: find the mean life of the system that needs all three. Repair costs 2 now and an expected 3.5 per year afterward, and replacement costs 15 now and an expected 0.7 per year: at a 5% discount rate, find the horizon in years at which the two present costs are equal.

Connections

Chapter 63 treated the principles immediately before these (1115–1119): accumulated consequences, path dependence, critical transitions, the cost of maintenance, and endurance against resilience; the source’s thirtieth thread repeats them word for word before continuing, so they are not restated here.

Chapter 57: Recovery, Regeneration, and Corrections That Hold

Recovery is a rate, and disturbances keep their own schedule.

Principles 840–849 deal with the limits of structural similarity, information preserved through transformations, identity and continuity, recovery after disturbance, regeneration, repair and adaptation, feedback control, resilience under repeated disturbances, redundancy, and long-term stability from local corrections. This chapter adds the arithmetic of repeated disturbance, the steady error of proportional control and how integral action removes it, and what structural similarity does and does not preserve.

Similar Structure, Different Systems

The source’s graph isomorphism, (u,v)∈E₁ exactly when (f(u),f(v))∈E₂, is the correct definition, and its caution is the important part: two networks with identical wiring can carry different flows, capacities and meanings. Its information claims are correct. An invertible map preserves information, the averaging example (2,4,6,8)→5 cannot be undone, a deterministic function cannot raise entropy (H(f(X))≤H(X)), and a chain X→Y→Z satisfies I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y) (Chapter 35). Its distinction between identity and continuity — a river or an organism keeps its identity through continual replacement of material — is the lineage view of Chapter 43.

Repeated Disturbances Accumulate

The source models recovery as dx/dt=−λx with time constant τ=1/λ, and says that disturbances arriving faster than τ prevent full recovery. That can be made exact. Suppose a system recovering at rate λ receives an equal kick u every T time units. Just after each kick the deviation approaches u/(1−e^(−λT)). With λ=0.1, kicks every 50 time units leave a peak only about 1.007u, essentially full recovery each time. Kicks every 10 time units raise the peak to about 1.58u, and every 5 to about 2.54u. No single disturbance changes, but their spacing determines whether they add up. As T becomes much shorter than τ, the peak grows roughly as τ/T times one kick. This is the quantitative form of the source’s failure mode of judging resilience from recovery after one isolated event. If λ itself declines under stress, as Chapter 60 described for slowing recovery near a threshold, accumulation grows faster still.

Figure 57.1. Left: deviation of a system recovering at rate λ=0.1 under equal kicks every 50, 10 and 5 time units; peaks settle at u/(1−e^(−λT)) ≈ 1.01u, 1.58u and 2.54u. Right: a first-order process dy/dt=−y+u tracking a unit target under proportional control (K_p=4, steady error 0.2) and proportional-integral control (K_p=4, K_i=2, error removed). Idealized models.

Proportional Correction Leaves a Steady Error

The source writes proportional control as u=K_p e and the PID law with integral and derivative terms. It does not show what the integral term is for.[95] For a simple process dy/dt=−y+u tracking a constant target r with u=K_p(r−y), the output settles at K_p r/(1+K_p). The remaining error is r/(1+K_p): half the target with K_p=1, a fifth with K_p=4, a tenth with K_p=9. Raising the gain shrinks the error but never removes it, and in real systems with delay a high gain eventually destabilizes the loop (Chapter 52). Adding an integral term, which keeps accumulating while any error remains, drives the steady error to zero for a constant target. That is why the source’s PID form is the standard design. The derivative term reacts to the rate of change and damps overshoot, but it amplifies measurement noise. In the source’s terms, correction that holds requires a memory of past error, not only a response to present error.

Repair, Regeneration, and Redundancy

The source’s regeneration balance dB/dt=S−D, with growth, steady maintenance or decline as S exceeds, equals or falls short of D, is Chapter 77’s renewal balance. Its distinction between repair, which restores a prior condition, and adaptation, which changes the organization, is sound. Its redundancy calculation, 1−(1−0.9)²=0.99, is correct and correctly conditioned on independent failure and successful switching. A third copy gives 0.999 under the same assumptions. Chapter 60 showed how even a small shared-cause loss caps such gains. Its discrete control condition, that every eigenvalue of A−BK must lie inside the unit circle, is correct. In one dimension it reduces to Chapter 52’s gain range.

Thesis

Resilience depends on recovery rate relative to the spacing of disturbances, a correction that responds only to present error leaves a permanent offset, and redundancy and repair protect only against failures that are independent of one another.

Place to Explore

For recovery rate λ=0.1 and equal kicks u every T time units, compute the settled peak deviation (in units of u) for T=50, 10 and 5. Then, for dy/dt=−y+u with proportional control u=K_p(1−y), give the steady error for K_p=1, 4 and 9, and state the steady error when an integral term is added.

Connections

Chapter 35 stated the data processing inequality, Chapter 43 identity through lineages, Chapter 20 degradation and recovery, Chapter 60 slowing recovery as an early warning, Chapter 77 renewal against deterioration, Chapter 55 and Chapter 60 redundancy and its limit under shared hazards, Chapter 52 feedback margins, and Chapter 52 the gain limit that the source’s condition |λ_i(A−BK)|<1 generalizes.

Chapter 58: Drift, Noise, and the Edge of Recovery

A small push repeated in one direction outlasts a large push that keeps changing its mind.

Principles 925–944 deal with energy and organization, equilibrium and dynamic stability, the accumulation of small changes, irreversible transformation, new forms from the breakdown of old ones, decay and renewal, recovery after catastrophic disturbance, survival and flourishing, uncertainty in long-term futures, responsibility toward successors, present choices and future possibilities, optionality, the danger of optimizing for one outcome, independent verification across generations, self-correcting systems, correction and reconstruction, preserving original evidence during revision, authority and verification, the limits of automated self-governance, and trustworthy continuity. Most of this movement restates earlier chapters. This chapter adds the two quantitative points the source states without working: when steady drift overtakes random fluctuation, and how a linear recovery model fails at the edge of the region where recovery works.

Drift Against Noise

The source writes accumulated change as X_n=X₀+ΣΔX_i (927) and says that changes pointing consistently in one direction accumulate, while changes that fluctuate independently around zero grow more slowly — in proportion to √n in a simple random-walk model. It treats the same sum with zero-mean steps in Principle 933, with Var(X_n)=nσ², which is correct for independent steps. The two cases combine. If each step has mean μ and standard deviation σ, the expected change after n steps is nμ, while the typical scatter is σ√n. Drift therefore dominates once n exceeds (σ/μ)². With μ=0.1 and σ=1, ten steps give an expected change of 1 against a scatter of about 3.2, so the trend is invisible. A hundred steps give 10 against 10. Ten thousand steps give 1,000 against 100. A bias too small to see in any short record becomes the main story over a long one. Conversely, a short run of apparent change can be pure noise. This is the arithmetic behind the source’s failure mode of judging a small change harmless by its immediate effect, and behind its distinction between systematic drift and random fluctuation.

Figure 58.1. Left: twenty seeded random walks with step mean 0.1 and standard deviation 1, with the drift line 0.1n and the band ±√n; the two cross at n=(σ/μ)²=100. Right: deviation after a disturbance under linear recovery dx/dt=−x and under dx/dt=−x+x³, which recovers only inside |x|<1; from x₀=1.1 the nonlinear system runs away at t≈0.88 while the linear model predicts return. Idealized models.

Recovery Has an Edge

The source models recovery as dx/dt=−λx and states the essential qualification: the model assumes the system remains within a region where the recovery mechanism works, and catastrophic disturbances can violate that assumption (931). A minimal nonlinear model makes the edge explicit. In dx/dt=−x+x³ the restoring rate is 1 near equilibrium, as in the linear model, but recovery holds only for |x|<1 (note 89). From x₀=0.5 the two models agree closely: the deviation falls to 0.05 in about 2.45 time units, against 2.30 for the linear model. From x₀=0.9 recovery slows markedly, taking about 3.72 units against 2.89, because the restoring force weakens near the edge. From x₀=1.1 the linear model still predicts return, but the nonlinear deviation grows without bound and diverges at t≈0.88. A recovery rate measured from small disturbances says nothing about where the edge lies. The source’s distinction among resistance, recovery, reorganization and transformation is the resilience framing of ecology,[96] and its eutrophication example is the hysteresis of Chapters 53 and 61, where reducing the load does not by itself restore the earlier state.

Options, Objectives, and Correction With Its Evidence

The source’s remaining formulas in this group are correctly qualified. The option value V_option=E[U | future information]−U_immediate commitment and the feasible-set update F_(t+1)=G(F_t,A_t,E_t) restate Chapter 82, including its warning that some opportunities vanish if action is postponed. Constrained optimization of J(x) subject to g_i(x)≤0 and the Pareto frontier of several objectives restate Chapters 54 and 82. (The source writes the multi-objective problem as max(J₁,…,J_m), which should be read as maximizing the vector of objectives, not the largest of them; its following sentence about the Pareto frontier shows that this is the intended meaning.) The stability condition for x_(t+1)=(A−BK)x_t is Chapter 52’s, and the source correctly calls it a condition for one class of systems. Its transition record T_i=(S_i,S_(i+1),A_i,E_i), with the warning that an append-only log does not make its contents true, restates Chapters 28 and 79. Its statements that authority is not verification (942) and that consistent execution is not correct judgment (943) restate Chapters 84 and 86. The conceptual sums such as T=I+P+A+V+C are kept as frameworks, as the source labels them.

Thesis

A steady bias overtakes random fluctuation after about (σ/μ)² steps, a recovery rate measured near equilibrium does not reveal where recovery stops, and options, objectives and corrections remain trustworthy only with their evidence and limits attached.

Place to Explore

For steps with mean 0.1 and standard deviation 1, give the expected change and the typical scatter after 10, 100 and 10,000 steps, and the crossover step count. Then, for dx/dt=−x+x³, find the time for the deviation to fall from 0.5 to 0.05 and from 0.9 to 0.05, compare each with the linear model dx/dt=−x, and find the time at which a deviation starting at 1.1 diverges.

Connections

Principles 920–924, which open the source thread, repeat material already integrated in Chapter 49 and are cross-referenced rather than repeated. Chapter 20 treated damped and critically damped motion and irreversible change, Chapters 10, 57 and 77 the renewal balance and turnover, Chapter 53 folds and hysteresis, Chapter 61 tipping and recovery, Chapter 82 option value, discounting and irreversibility as a constraint, Chapters 54 and 82 Pareto trade-offs, Chapter 29 Goodhart’s law, Chapters 64 and 65 independent verification, Chapters 52 and 57 the discrete stability condition on A−BK, Chapters 28 and 79 append-only records and bounded repair, Chapter 84 delegated and automated authority, and Chapter 67 the evidential status UNKNOWN.

Chapter 59: Balance, Correction, and Two Ways to Measure Resilience

Losing less at first and losing less in total are different achievements.

Principles 990–999 deal with equilibrium and dynamic balance, feedback in maintaining higher-order organization, the limits of self-organization, complexity and fragility, when a stable pattern becomes a new system, maintenance and emergence, disturbances that reorganize systems, resilience and resistance, changing without losing viability, and the threshold between continuity and transformation. The source is careful throughout and labels its models as illustrative. This chapter adds how long a dynamic balance takes to respond, why the source’s warning about excessive correction needs sampling or delay to be true, what the source’s two resilience ratios leave out, and how a weighted continuity score can hide the loss of an essential property.

A Balance That Is Not Rest

The source writes a balanced quantity as dX/dt=P−D, stable when production matches loss even though both continue, and warns that an unchanged measurement does not show that a system is healthy or inactive (990). A simple version shows how much a steady reading hides. Let production be constant at P=10 units per day and loss proportional to the stock, D=kX with k=0.1 per day. The steady stock is X*=P/k=100 units, and each unit stays on average 1/k=10 days, so the whole stock is replaced every ten days or so while the reading stays at 100. If production halves to 5, the stock relaxes as X(t)=50+50e^(−0.1t) and covers 95% of the way to its new level of 50 only after ln(20)/0.1≈30 days. A stock replaced every ten years would show the same steady reading of 100 and take about thirty years to respond to the same change. The steady reading alone does not distinguish them; the flows and the response time do. The source’s maintenance balance dQ/dt=M+G−D (995) has the same structure.

When Stronger Correction Destabilizes

The source’s feedback model is dx/dt=ax+bu with u=−Kx, giving dx/dt=(a−bK)x, which converges when a−bK<0 (991). This is correct, and the source rightly says real systems add delays, noise and constraints. It then warns that too much corrective action can produce oscillation or instability. In the model as written that cannot happen: increasing K only makes a−bK more negative and the return faster. The warning becomes true once the correction is applied at discrete times or after a delay, which is how real controllers act. If the control is updated every Δ time units and held in between, the exact sampled system is x_(n+1)=φx_n with φ=e^(aΔ)−K(b/a)(e^(aΔ)−1). For a=0.5, b=1 and Δ=0.1, it is stable only for 0.5<K<20.0; at K=25 the factor is about −1.51, and each correction overshoots by more than the last. Chapter 52 developed the delayed version of the same effect. The scope limit is that the overcorrection warning belongs to the sampled or delayed system, not to the continuous one-dimensional model the source writes down.

Complexity and Series Failure

The source’s series reliability R_system=p^N, with ten independent required components at 0.99 giving about 0.904, is correct and is Chapter 3’s calculation; at a hundred components the same reliability gives about 0.366. The source correctly limits it to independent failures in a strict series architecture and adds common-cause failure (993), which Chapters 31 and 60 quantified. Its point that self-organization produces order without guaranteeing accuracy or benefit (992), and its conditions S=f(O,B,I,R,P) for a pattern to count as a system (994), restate Chapters 40 and 43.

Resistance, Recovery, and the Loss in Between

The source separates resistance, the ability to limit change during a disturbance, from resilience, the ability to recover or reorganize afterwards, and gives two illustrative measures: resistance R_s=1−ΔQ/Q₀ and relative recovery R_r=Q(t)/Q₀ (997). Both are snapshots. Consider two systems with initial performance Q₀=100. System A drops to 90 (R_s=0.9) and recovers slowly, Q(t)=100−10e^(−0.1t) with t in days. System B drops to 60 (R_s=0.6) and recovers quickly, Q(t)=100−40e^(−t). At half a day A’s recovery ratio is about 0.905 and B’s about 0.757; at three days A’s is about 0.926 and B’s about 0.980. The ratios are equal at t=ln4/0.9≈1.54 days, so which system looks more resilient depends on when R_r is read. The total performance lost, the area between Q₀ and Q(t), is 10/0.1=100 performance-days for A and 40/1=40 for B: the less resistant system loses less overall. Engineering resilience frameworks measure this area, not only the depth or the endpoint,[97] and the source’s two ratios should be reported with it and with the time at which R_r was read. The source’s own qualification that formal measures depend on the system and the performance variable is correct; the loss area is one such measure, not a universal one.

Figure 59.1. Left: performance of a resistant but slow-recovering system A (drop to 90, recovery rate 0.1 per day) and a less resistant, fast-recovering system B (drop to 60, rate 1 per day); the shaded areas are their total losses, 100 and 40 performance-days, and their recovery ratios cross at about 1.54 days. Right: weighted continuity scores for two transformations of the same system; both score 0.70, but the second has lost its purpose, an essential property. Illustrative values.

Viability and the Threshold of Transformation

The source’s viable region V={x: g_i(x)≤0, i=1,…,m}, and its point that the region itself can move when the environment changes (998), are Chapter 54’s viability as a set of constraints. Its table separating maintenance, resistance, recovery, adaptation and transformation is a useful vocabulary and is kept.

For the threshold between continuity and transformation (999), the source defines a weighted continuity measure C(t)=Σw_j s_j(t)/Σw_j over essential properties, says plainly that it is a conceptual model and not an established measure of identity, and requires that the essential properties be defined before the evaluation. Those qualifications are right, and one more follows from the formula. A weighted average lets properties compensate for one another. Give a system five properties with weights lineage 0.2, function 0.3, materials 0.1, governance 0.2 and purpose 0.2. If its materials and governance are replaced while the rest is preserved, C=0.7. If instead its materials are replaced and its purpose is lost, C is again 0.7. The score is identical, but by the source’s own account the second case may be a successor rather than the original system. Properties declared essential therefore need their own floor, such as s_j≥s_min for function and purpose, checked separately from the average, which is Chapter 54’s distinction between a constraint and a trade-off and Chapter 90’s warning about weights.

Thesis

A steady reading conceals the flows and response time behind it, stronger correction destabilizes only when it is sampled or delayed, and resilience and continuity need more than one number: the loss accumulated during recovery and a separate check on every essential property.

Place to Explore

For system A (Q(t)=100−10e^(−0.1t)) and system B (Q(t)=100−40e^(−t)), find the time at which their recovery ratios are equal and their total losses in performance-days. Then, for the sampled controller with a=0.5, b=1 and Δ=0.1, find the range of K that is stable and the factor φ at K=25.

Connections

Much of it restates other chapters: Chapters 3 and 4 treated steady states maintained by flows, Chapter 52 feedback gain, delay and overcorrection, Chapter 3 the reliability of series systems, Chapters 31 and 60 common-cause failure, Chapter 54 viability as a set of constraints, Chapters 57 and 58 recovery and its limits, and Chapters 43 and 80 identity criteria.

Chapter 60: Early Warnings, Reconstruction, and Records That Outlive Us

A warning signal is a hypothesis about recovery; a surviving record is a hypothesis about meaning.

The source’s Principles 563–567 and 569–574 concern civilizational collapse, early-warning signals, the limits of historical prediction, reconstruction of lost societies, long-term survival of knowledge, scientific transmission, languages, technological fragility, knowledge outliving its creators, the physics of storage, and the limits of digital immortality. This chapter adds the quantitative pieces.

Collapse Through Dependencies

The source represents a society as a dependency network in which each subsystem’s condition x_i depends on its own dynamics, on the condition of others through coupling a_ij, and on outside support u_i. The equation is a framework, not a fitted model. Its lesson is the one Chapters 39 and 40 developed for physical networks: assessing each institution separately misses the dependencies that carry a failure from one to another, and functional collapse can precede physical destruction.

What Slower Recovery Looks Like, and What It Does Not Prove

For the simple Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model dx=−λx dt+σdW the source gives the stationary variance σ²/(2λ) and lag-one autocorrelation e^(−λΔt). Both are correct. With σ=1 and Δt=1, a recovery rate falling from λ=0.5 to 0.1 raises the variance from 1 to 5 and the autocorrelation from 0.607 to 0.905.[98]

The inverse inference is weaker. Variance also rises if disturbances grow, autocorrelation rises if sampling becomes more frequent or the series is smoothed, and some transitions are not preceded by slowing at all (Chapter 2). Estimates are also noisy: for an AR(1) series the large-sample standard error of the lag-one autocorrelation is about √((1−ρ²)/n), roughly 0.11 for ρ=0.607 and n=50 observations. A short social or institutional record may be unable to distinguish a modest change in recovery from noise. Treat a rising indicator as a reason for closer measurement and for testing recovery directly, not as a forecast of collapse.

Historical prediction has a further limit the source names: P(C_{t+1}|X_t,H_t) depends on whether past cases are comparable, and historical analogy is not historical law.

Reconstruction and Transmission

The source writes surviving evidence as Y=h(X)+ε. When h(X₁)=h(X₂) for different pasts, no amount of analysis of Y alone can choose between them (Chapter 26). Reconstruction of a lost civilization therefore needs independent lines of evidence, explicit uncertainty, and alternatives kept open.

Knowledge survives only if the chain from discovery through documentation, transmission, interpretation, and reproduction remains intact. Reproducing a result needs data, method, experimental environment, computational configuration, and standards (Chapter 66). The source’s own example is apt: candidate exponents N^(−2/3), N^(−1), and N^(−2) for the strand ensemble remain competing hypotheses until finite-size checks separate them (Chapter 72). Languages and notations need their symbol inventory, rules, meaning, and context (Chapter 32). The source’s net-resilience expression C−αD−βK, in which dependency complexity D and common-mode exposure K subtract from capability C, is a framework with weights to be justified, not a score.

Figure 60.1. Left: in the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model, stationary variance σ²/2λ and lag-one autocorrelation e^(−λ) rise as recovery rate λ falls (σ=1, Δt=1). Right: survival over 1,000 intervals for one copy (p=0.999 each), three independently failing copies audited and repaired every interval, and the same three copies with a shared-cause loss probability of 10⁻⁴ per interval. Models under stated assumptions.

Copies Survive Only If Someone Keeps Repairing Them

The source’s example of an unmaintained record is correct: survival probability 0.999 per interval gives 0.999^1000≈0.368 after 1,000 independent intervals, and the source warns that real failures are correlated. Maintenance changes the calculation. Suppose three copies each fail independently with probability 0.001 per interval, and every interval an audit detects loss and restores from a surviving copy. The record is lost only if all three fail in the same interval, probability 10⁻⁹, so it survives 1,000 intervals with probability about 1−10⁻⁶.

Add a shared cause—common credentials, software, site, power, or key—that destroys all copies together with probability 10⁻⁴ per interval. Survival falls to about (1−10⁻⁴)^1000≈0.905. The shared cause dominates; more independent copies cannot repair it (Chapter 41). And survival of bits is not survival of knowledge: the record must still be readable, interpretable, and verifiable (Chapter 5). Storage itself is physical. A system with N distinguishable states holds at most log₂N bits, and logically irreversible erasure has a minimum energy cost (Chapter 22).

Thesis

Collective knowledge outlives its creators through maintained, independently failing copies, interpretable context, and reproducible methods. Warning indicators and historical analogies support closer examination, not certainty.

Place to Explore

For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model with λ=0.2, σ=1, and Δt=1, compute the stationary variance, the lag-one autocorrelation, and its approximate standard error for n=100. Then compute survival over 2,000 intervals for one copy with p=0.9995, for two copies failing independently with probability 0.0005 and audited each interval, and for those two copies with a shared-cause loss probability of 5×10⁻⁵.

Connections

Chapter 2 cautioned that critical slowing down is not universal, Chapter 26 treated non-identifiable reconstruction, Chapter 41 common-mode copies, Chapter 32 meaning across future observers, and Chapter 66 recovered experiments.

Chapter 61: Tipping, Recovery, and Unfinished Creation

A system that has tipped may need far more help to return than it needed to stay.

The source’s Principles 629–638 concern unfinished creation, ecological tipping points, recovery of damaged ecosystems, technology and natural systems, planetary stewardship, unfinished questions, creative evolution, cultural diversity, memory and imagination, and new forms of meaning. Principle 628 is a gap: the preview announced “the mathematics of planetary feedback,” but the thread supplies only two short narrative formulations of 628—continuation of the unfinished, X_{t+1}=F(X_t,E_t,U_t), and unfinished creation as inheritance plus discovery plus transformation—with no structured development. The previewed titles also shifted: tipping points, recovery, technology, and stewardship appear as 630–633.

The Source’s Simple Model Does Not Tip

The source introduces tipping points with dx/dt=rx(1−x/K)−dx, a logistic population with a proportional loss rate d, and then says more complicated systems can switch between alternative stable states. The qualification needs to be sharper. In this model the equilibrium is x*=K(1−d/r) for d<r and zero otherwise. With r=0.5 and K=1000, a loss rate of 0.25 leaves 500 and 0.45 leaves 100; the population declines smoothly as d approaches r, and reducing d restores it along the same path. There is a threshold at d=r, but no abrupt jump and no hysteresis.

A fixed loss behaves differently. With a constant harvest H, Chapter 47 found two equilibria merging at H=rK/4=125. Raise the harvest past 125 and the stock collapses from about 500 even though the change was small. Lowering the harvest back to 120 does not reverse the damage if the stock has already fallen below that quota’s threshold of 400: at a stock of 350 regeneration is only 0.5×350×0.65≈114, so the decline continues. The harvest must fall below about 114 before the stock grows again. This path dependence—recovery needs more than reversing the push—is what distinguishes a tipping point with hysteresis.[99] Lakes, reefs, and forests may or may not show it; the source correctly says transitions are system-specific and not every tipping point is irreversible.

Figure 61.1. Left: under proportional loss d the equilibrium K(1−d/r) declines smoothly to zero at d=r (r=0.5, K=1000). Right: under a constant harvest H the stable and unstable equilibria meet at H=125; beyond it the stock collapses, and at 350 regeneration (about 114) is below a quota of 120. Idealized models.

Recovery Produces Successors, Not Originals

A damaged system follows X₀→X_d→X_r, and the source stresses that the recovered state may differ from the original. Even in the logistic model without harvest, recovery takes time: from 50 to 900 with r=0.5 and K=1000 takes t=(1/r)ln[x₁(K−x₀)/(x₀(K−x₁))]≈10.3 years. Real recovery may also require restoring species composition, habitat structure, functions, and relationships, any of which can be lost when abundance returns (Chapter 20). Technology that depends on energy, materials, water, land, and maintenance time remains inside these systems, not outside them (Chapters 5 and 54). Stewardship needs knowledge, legitimate authority, resources, accountability, and attention to future generations (Chapters 82 and 84–86).

Unfinished Questions and Creative Change

The source treats creation as an evolving state, M_{t+1}=T(M_t,Δ_t), and creative evolution as variation filtered by selection or evaluation. These are frameworks: they say what to record—what was inherited, what was added, and by what evaluation—without predicting outcomes. Unfinished scientific questions should be handed on with observations, models, and unresolved uncertainty, as Chapter 72 recommended for rival hypotheses. Cultural traditions persist through language, oral and written forms, practices, access, and the freedom to reinterpret; their diversity plays the portfolio role of Chapter 50, keeping more than one way of meeting future conditions. Imagination draws on memory, present perception, and generative recombination, and meaning depends on symbol, context, history, and interpreter (Chapter 32). The source’s accounting I_{n+1}=I_n+ΔK+ΔC+ΔM is additive only as metaphor; losses belong in it too (Chapter 60).

Thesis

Thresholds matter most where systems have hysteresis: there, prevention is cheaper than recovery, and what returns is a successor that must be evaluated on its own terms. Unfinished work persists when its inheritance, additions, and open questions are recorded together.

Place to Explore

For r=0.5 and K=1000, find the equilibrium under proportional loss d=0.3 and the loss rate that leaves 200. Then, under a constant harvest, find the regeneration at a stock of 300 and the largest quota that still lets that stock grow. Finally, compute the logistic recovery time from 100 to 800 without harvest.

Connections

Planetary feedback is not reconstructed here; Chapters 47 and 50 contain the feedback models the source did develop.

Chapter 62: Hidden Depletion, Delayed Limits, and Environments That Remember

Output can stay level for years while the reserve beneath it runs out.

Principles 1135–1143 deal with hidden depletion of reserves, carrying capacity, renewal rates, overshoot and collapse, the difference between growth and flourishing, the mathematics of sustainable balance, feedback between systems and their environments, ecological memory, and the recovery of lost complexity. This chapter adds the time a reserve buys before output must fall, a correction to the source’s delayed-capacity model and the thresholds of the standard delayed logistic, and what a single recovered indicator can and cannot certify.

Stability Borrowed From the Future

The source says that a system can keep its visible output while consuming the reserves that make future output possible (1135). It writes dR/dt=I−C and notes the dangerous interval in which R is still above a critical R_min while the trajectory is already unsustainable. The interval has a length. With constant consumption C above replenishment I, the time from R₀ to R_min is (R₀−R_min)/(C−I). A reserve of 1000 drawn at a net 20 per period (consumption 60, replenishment 40) reaches a floor of 200 after 40 periods, and output can stay at 60 for that entire time. At the floor it must fall to the income of 40. Nothing in the output record before period 40 shows the decline. Only a measurement of the reserve does. That is the source’s failure mode, measuring production instead of reserves, and its examples—aquifers, soil organic matter, deferred maintenance, exhausted staff—are cases where the reserve is the hard thing to measure.

Figure 62.1. Left: a reserve of 1000 drawn at consumption 60 against replenishment 40 reaches the floor of 200 at period 40 while output stays level, then output drops to the income of 40. Right: the delayed logistic dN/dt=rN(1−N(t−τ)/K) from N=0.1K: rτ=0.3 rises without overshoot, rτ=1.0 overshoots to about 1.28K and settles, rτ=2.0 cycles between about 0.07K and 2.9K. Idealized models.

Carrying Capacity and Renewal

The source’s logistic model dN/dt=rN(1−N/K) is stated correctly, and so is the qualification that matters: K is conditional, rising or falling with climate, technology, competition, disease and degradation (1136). The plain logistic cannot overshoot. Started below K it approaches K monotonically. The source’s remark that overshoot happens “especially when feedback is delayed” is therefore not a footnote but the mechanism. Its renewal balance ΔR=(G−U)Δt, with the reserve rising, steady or falling as G exceeds, equals or falls short of U, is correct as a constant-rate approximation (1137). Its distinction between recovery of quantity and recovery of quality is taken up below. Its mathematics of sustainable balance (1140) repeats, correctly, the logistic-harvest results: regeneration rR(1−R/K) peaks at rK/4 when R=K/2, and a positive equilibrium under constant use U requires U≤rK/4. It adds the right warning that a mathematically possible equilibrium is not automatically safe. The derivation, and the instability of the lower equilibrium, are in Chapter 47 and Chapter 61 and are not repeated here.

Overshoot Needs a Delay in the Right Place

To model overshoot the source writes dN/dt=rN(1−N(t)/K(t−τ)), a carrying capacity “as experienced after a delay” (1138). As written, the delay acts only when K itself changes: with a constant K, K(t−τ)=K and the model reduces to the ordinary logistic, which never overshoots. The standard delayed logistic, due to Hutchinson, puts the delay in the density feedback: dN/dt=rN(1−N(t−τ)/K).[100] Its behavior depends only on the product rτ. For rτ below 1/e≈0.368 the approach to K is monotonic. Between 1/e and π/2≈1.571 the population overshoots and settles through damped oscillations. Above π/2 the equilibrium is unstable and the population cycles indefinitely.[101] Started at a tenth of K, rτ=1 gives a first peak near 1.28K before settling, and rτ=2 gives a cycle between about 0.07K and 2.9K. With r=0.5 per year, a two-year delay gives rτ=1 and a four-year delay rτ=2. The threshold π/2 is the same one that bounds delayed negative feedback in Chapter 52. The source’s label “illustrative, not a universal law of collapse” is right, and the corrected model shows what the illustration needs: a delay between the population and the feedback it feels, not between the environment and its own value.

Growth Is Not Flourishing

The source says that expansion measures how much a system grows, while flourishing concerns the quality and sustainability of what it becomes (1139). It writes F=f(G,H,Q,R,E), explicitly not a standardized equation, and connects its failure mode—optimizing a measurable quantity while neglecting its purpose—to Goodhart’s law. That is Chapter 29’s and Chapter 90’s proxy failure, and the source states it correctly.

The Environment Feeds Back

The source says that systems change the environments that then act on them, writes the coupled pair dS/dt=f(S,E), dE/dt=g(E,S), and names the evolutionary form of the idea, niche construction (1141). The term is correct: organisms modify their surroundings in ways that change selection on themselves and their descendants, as with beaver dams, coral reefs and soil built by roots.[102] Its failure mode, treating the environment as a fixed resource supply, is what the delayed logistic makes quantitative, since a population that degrades its own K is a coupled system whose capacity is a state variable, not a constant.

Ecological Memory

The source uses the term ecological memory for the way surviving organisms, biological legacies and altered conditions carry the influence of past events into recovery: seeds in the soil, living roots, surviving trees, soil chemistry, microorganisms, changed light and moisture (1142). The term is used in this sense in the forest-resilience literature, which also stresses the source’s caution: when disturbances change in kind, frequency or severity, the legacies a system depended on can be lost, and the memory stops matching the disturbance.[103] Its statement that environmental memory is selective—some traces survive, some are transformed, some vanish—is the incomplete record of Chapter 21 applied to an ecosystem.

Recovered Appearance, Unrecovered Relations

The source says that returning to an earlier appearance does not necessarily restore the original system (1143). It describes a condition by several dimensions, Q=(S,F,D,R,H) for structure, function, diversity, resilience and historical continuity, labelled conceptual. The examples are the right ones. Two forests with similar canopy cover can differ in species composition, soil microbes, age distribution, connectivity and regeneration potential. Its failure mode, using one indicator as proof of complete restoration, is the reason Chapter 59 needed two measures even for resilience, resistance and recovery: a recovered indicator certifies only itself. Chapter 61 showed that a tipped system usually recovers to a successor state, not to the original. A restoration report should name the dimensions it measured and say which it did not.

Thesis

Level output says nothing about the reserve beneath it, overshoot requires a delay between a population and the limit it feels, and a recovered indicator certifies only itself; continuity is judged by reserves, by delays and by the dimensions that were actually measured.

Place to Explore

A reserve of 1000 is drawn at 60 per period and replenished at 40. How many periods pass before it reaches a floor of 200, and what must output fall to then? For the delayed logistic dN/dt=rN(1−N(t−τ)/K) with r=0.5 per year, classify the approach to K for delays of 0.5, 2 and 4 years using the thresholds rτ=1/e and rτ=π/2.

Connections

Chapter 47 derived the maximum sustainable yield rK/4 and the two equilibria under a constant harvest, and Chapter 61 showed the collapse and hysteresis when the harvest crosses that maximum. Chapter 6 corrected the source’s inequality U≤G as a test of stability, Chapter 52 gave the gain and delay limits of feedback, and Chapter 59 two ways to measure resilience.

Chapter 63: Agreement on Tests, Lingering States, and the Limits of Equivalence

Passing every test that was run says nothing about the tests that were not.

Principles 1100–1119 deal with scale, collective behavior, information loss, reconstruction, the limits of equivalence, emergence across scales, collective memory, the survival of rules, changing environments, adaptation and optimization, feedback across generations, evolutionary tradeoffs, the limits of prediction, the preservation of possibility, the unfinished system, the accumulation of consequences, path dependence, critical transitions, the cost of maintenance, and the difference between endurance and resilience. This chapter adds two calculations: why agreement at every tested point does not establish equivalence, and why a system that has just crossed a tipping point can look unchanged for a long time.

Scale, Information, and Reconstruction

The source’s ratio t/τ for whether change is visible at a given scale (1100) is Chapter 2’s observation window, and its coupled-component equations dx_i/dt=f_i(x_i)+Σa_ijg_ij(x_i,x_j) (1101, 1105) are Chapters 8 and 40. Its Shannon entropy and data processing inequality, I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y) for a chain X→Y→Z, with the remark that a hash shows whether a file changed but cannot restore what was lost before the hash was taken (1102), are Chapters 22, 23, 35 and 57. Its inverse problem y=F(x)+ϵ with estimate x_hat=F⁻¹(y), and its warning that the inverse may not exist or may not be unique (1103), are Chapter 26’s observability; its four labels, observed, inferred, estimated and unknown, match Chapter 67’s evidential statuses and are kept.

Agreement on Tests Is Not Equivalence

The source separates visual, functional, structural, historical and informational equivalence, and notes that two machines can produce the same output on a limited set of inputs while having different internal architectures, F₁(x_i)=F₂(x_i) at the tested points without F₁(x)=F₂(x) everywhere (1104). A simple construction shows how little finite agreement constrains. Let F₁(x)=x and F₂(x)=x+0.1·x(x−1)(x−2)(x−3). The two agree exactly at the four tested inputs 0, 1, 2 and 3, because the added term vanishes there. Between tests they differ slightly: at x=1.5, F₂ is about 1.556 against 1.5. Outside the tested range they diverge: at x=4, F₂ is 6.4 against 4, and at x=5 it is 17 against 5. Any function that vanishes at the tested points can be added in the same way, so agreement on n tests identifies a system only within a class assumed in advance, for example polynomials of degree below n, which n points determine uniquely. This is the formal content of the source’s rule that equivalence must name the property and the domain tested, of Chapter 75’s model that fails outside its tested range, and of Chapter 74’s bridged standards. The source’s graph isomorphism example, structural equivalence without shared history, is correct.

Rules, Environments, and Correction

The source’s knowledge balance for collective memory (1106) is Chapter 33’s. Its invariants, dE_total/dt=0 and I(T(x))=I(x), and its warning that preserving a rule does not make the rule right (1107), are Chapters 10 and 43. Its changing-environment viability set (1108), its separation of adaptation from optimization, x*=arg max J(x), with the requirement to state the objective, constraints and timescale (1109), its coupled system and environment S_(t+1)=F(S_t,E_t), E_(t+1)=G(E_t,S_t) (1110), and its energy budget across maintenance, growth, reproduction and defence (1111) are Chapters 47, 54, 58 and 90. Its prediction horizon δ(t)≈δ₀e^(λt) (1112) is Chapter 53. Its feasible-futures and option-value relations (1113) are Chapters 33, 58 and 82. Its closed-loop correction x_(t+1)=(A−BK)x_t (1114) is Chapter 59’s result that correction which is too strong destabilizes; the source’s condition that the eigenvalues of A−BK lie inside the unit circle is correct. Its accumulation of independent changes, with variance nσ² and spread √n·σ (1115), is Chapter 58’s drift against noise; its path dependence S_(t+1)=F(S_t,H_t,E_t) (1116) is Chapter 53’s.

A Tipping Point That Looks Like Nothing

The source writes the saddle-node normal form dx/dt=r+x², with equilibria x*=±√(−r) for r<0, one stable and one unstable, which meet at r=0 and vanish for r>0 (1117). The stable one is x*=−√(−r), and its recovery rate is 2√(−r), which falls to zero at the fold: this is Chapter 60’s critical slowing down. The same model shows what happens just after the threshold is crossed. For small positive r there is no equilibrium, but the system passes slowly through the region where the equilibria used to be, the “ghost” of the vanished state. The time to pass through it is about π/√r (note 89). For r=0.01 that is about 31 time units, and for r=0.0001 about 314: the closer the crossing, the longer the system lingers looking almost as it did before. A system that has already crossed a tipping point can therefore appear stable for a long time, and an absence of visible change after a threshold is crossed is weak evidence that it was not crossed. The source’s qualifications, that early-warning indicators are not universal and that not every abrupt change reveals a hidden tipping point, are correct and kept. The normal form is a local model near the fold, not a calibrated description of any lake, climate or market.

Figure 63.1. Left: F₁(x)=x and F₂(x)=x+0.1x(x−1)(x−2)(x−3) agree at the four tested inputs 0–3 and diverge outside them. Right: trajectories of dx/dt=r+x² from x=−10 for r=0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001, just past the fold; each lingers near x=0, the ghost of the vanished equilibrium, for about π/√r before escaping. Idealized models.

Maintenance, Endurance, and Resilience

The source’s maintenance balance dQ/dt=M(t)−D(t), its decomposition of future cost into routine, deferred and failure costs (1118), and its reminder that ΔS_total≥0 are Chapters 20 and 55. Its separation of endurance from resilience, R=f(E_s,R_s,C_r,A_d), with the warning that longevity is not proof of success (1119), is Chapter 59’s distinction between resisting and recovering.

Thesis

Agreement at every tested point fixes a system only within an assumed class, and a system that has just passed a fold can linger near its vanished state for a time that grows as the crossing becomes more marginal, so neither equivalence nor stability can be read from the tests and observations that happened to be made.

Place to Explore

For F₁(x)=x and F₂(x)=x+0.1x(x−1)(x−2)(x−3), confirm that they agree at x=0, 1, 2 and 3, and compute both at x=1.5, 4 and 5. Then, for dx/dt=r+x², find the recovery rate at the stable equilibrium for r=−0.01, and the bottleneck passage time π/√r for r=0.01 and r=0.0001.

Connections

Most of this restates earlier chapters, and the source is careful throughout: Chapter 2 treated observation windows and timescales, Chapters 8 and 40 coupled components and collective order, Chapters 22, 35 and 57 information loss and the data processing inequality, Chapter 26 reconstruction and observability, Chapter 33 knowledge balances, Chapters 10 and 43 invariants and conservation laws, Chapters 53 and 54 changing environments and viability, Chapters 54 and 58 tradeoffs and optionality, Chapter 47 inherited commons, Chapter 53 sensitive dependence and prediction horizons, Chapter 59 correction that becomes too strong, Chapter 58 drift against noise, Chapters 53 and 60 folds, hysteresis and slowing recovery, Chapters 20 and 55 maintenance, and Chapter 59 resistance against recovery.
